summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia, of which Tolima is a department, is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Courts have also intervened directly in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Targeted killings of trans people continue in ordinary urban settings. El País English edition (14 April 2025) reports that Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon and no one had been arrested. The same report states that hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and that her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was"; President Petro ordered an urgent investigation.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate. The Guardian investigation (30 July 2024) documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating "social cleansing" flyers against trans women, and quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. The report gives 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

No finding specific to Tolima on law, enforcement practice or incidents for trans people appears in the sources. The two incident reports available concern Antioquia and Caquetá, other departments elsewhere in Colombia. Nothing in the record marks Tolima as materially different from the national picture, and nothing marks it as safer; the department is assessed against the national transfemicide and armed-group baseline set out above.
tangentialFactors:
The violence documented in the sources falls into two distinct settings, and a visitor's exposure differs accordingly. One is the ordinary urban daylight assault recorded in Bello, Antioquia, where onlookers filmed rather than intervened and where no arrest followed in the month after the killing. The other is territory under armed-group control, where killings are announced in advance through flyer campaigns and framed as "social cleansing".

Named departments function as data points on a national pattern rather than as isolated localities: Caquetá for the week-long ultimatum and flyer campaign against trans women, Guajira for a posted kill list naming individuals, Antioquia for the urban attack. Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond sex work, and Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men.

Prosecution practice cuts against victims at the investigative stage. An activist quoted by The Guardian states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases, which affects how cause and motive are established. Against that, the Special Jurisdiction for Peace's July 2023 indictment of 15 former rebels shows conflict-era violence against LGBT people being treated as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

International scrutiny is active and recent. Graeme Reid's May 2025 mission praised Colombia's legal reforms while stating that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, a formulation that applies to any department, Tolima included.

Whether armed groups operate in Tolima, circulate flyers there, or have issued threats against trans residents is unresolved on this record; the armed-group violence documented here comes from Caquetá and Guajira.
